webTitle: ‘Trump? I think he’s a disaster’: Ohio voters aggrieved as president prepares to visit

fields.headline: ‘Trump? I think he’s a disaster’: Ohio voters aggrieved as president prepares to visit
fields.trailText: President’s popularity has plummeted in solidly Republican state – will his presence at midterm rallies help or hinder?
fields.bodyText: Kelly Savage-Radich grew up in a Republican-supporting Ohio family and voted for Donald Trump in 2016 and 2020. But today the mother of three, who lives in a Montgomery county suburb of Dayton, is facing the prospect of having to sell one of her family’s vehicles due to the high cost of gas. Her grocery bill has gone up about $100 a week. She lays the blame squarely at the Trump administration’s door. “He wants his name on everything,” she said. “I’m sorry, but I don’t give a shit whose name is on the Kennedy Center.” That wasn’t the only matter on her list of grievances – Savage-Radich also brought up the killing of Renee Good in Minneapolis earlier this year. She said: “The shooting of an American citizen dead in the street, and no one was held accountable? I have two daughters, and I’m trying to teach them all the freedoms this country has, but it feels like our freedoms are being taken. “For people that always claim, ‘Don’t tread on me,’ they sure have no problem now.” On Saturday, Trump will visit Montgomery county, which he only barely lost in 2024, to rally for two Republicans struggling in key Ohio election races: incumbent US senator Jon Husted, and Vivek Ramaswamy, the candidate for Ohio governor. Ohio has been solidly Republican for more than a decade. Trump won Ohio by handy margins in the past three presidential elections, and the state has not voted for a Democratic president since Barack Obama in 2012. The Republican party holds a supermajority in the state’s legislature. But the president’s popularity in the industrial midwestern state has plummeted during his second term, and his presence may be more of a hindrance than a help. A Marist poll of nearly 1,300 registered Ohio voters conducted late last month found that 56% of participants disapprove of the job Trump is doing as president. In two important primaries held earlier this year, turnout for Republicans in Montgomery county was just two-thirds of that for Democrats. In last May’s Republican gubernatorial primary, turnout was down 33% or 362,000 votes compared to the previous primary, held in 2022. In a US Senate race that could help decide which party controls the national political landscape, Husted is polling behind his Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown. Despite Ohio electing Republican governors in six out of the past seven elections, Ramaswamy, a billionaire former Republican presidential candidate who until recently was one of Trump’s most vocal supporters, is also polling behind Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate. Other prominent Ohio Republicans have been in the headlines recently for all the wrong reasons. Representative Max Miller, who until domestic and child abuse allegations against him emerged last summer enjoyed close ties with Trump, faces stiff opposition to retain his congressional seat from a union ironworker. (Miller has denied all of the allegations, and has not faced criminal charges. The House ethics committee is investigating the allegations.) Montgomery county, a mix of urban, suburban and rural communities, has been a swing county for decades: in the presidential election two years ago, Trump lost it by just 1,201 votes, one of just seven of 88 counties in Ohio to fall Democratic nominee Kamala Harris’s way. With the midterms just a month away, the county’s leading Republicans admit that they’re in a fight. “You know, it’s been slower [than in previous election cycles], but it’s picking up. Honestly, I haven’t seen much energy on either side, but we’re getting more interest, people are getting engaged,” said Phil Plummer, the chair of the Montgomery county Republican party and a member of the Ohio house of representatives. “Obviously our candidates knocking on doors are hearing about the affordability issues. But we tell them: we didn’t create that, the Democrats did, and it’s hard to fix it in two years.” Plummer said that during the Biden administration too much money was printed in the form of hundreds of billions of dollars in federal tax breaks and investment spending, which has fueled higher costs today. Democrats say Biden’s spending surge was to combat the economic recession caused by the 2020 pandemic and point to Trump’s war on Iran costing Americans more than $44bn. “Obviously, the war [on Iran] hasn’t helped as far as oil prices, but Ohio has been deemed the number one state to do business in the nation. We’re moving the ball in Ohio; we’ve lowered property tax and cut income tax,” he said. “So we’re doing the best we can.” Few residents care to talk politics in the neighborhoods of Dayton, Montgomery county’s largest city. “Trump? I think he’s a disaster,” said a woman who declined to give her name as she stood outside a tattoo parlor in the Old North district, a working-class area north of downtown Dayton. Caring for his invalid mother on the porch of his home, Bill, a former nurse and Republican voter who asked not to be fully identified in order to speak freely, disagreed, and said the wider focus on rising gas prices was misplaced. “It’s always been crazy high, and people will buy a whole lot of gas at $2.99 but act like it’s out of control when it’s $3,” he says, adding that he has not decided whether he will vote in the midterms yet. “It seems like everybody is making more money, even with the most menial jobs.” Independents are set to play a major role in deciding Ohio’s next governor and the senate race between Husted and Brown. Nearly 38% of Ohio voters, or 2.9 million people, are independents, according to the Independent Voter Project. Running as an independent candidate for US house of representatives, Sandeep Dixit has knocked on hundreds of doors and met thousands of Ohioans on the campaign trail in north-east Ohio’s 13th district. He says the biggest issue voters are talking about is the hate-filled language coming from the political class. “People understand that if we continue with extreme positions the country’s going to get torn apart,” he said. “That’s the number one issue.” Dixit wouldn’t say for which parties he voted in the past but believes that Ohio Republicans have done well on the rule of law. However, “when it comes to being empathetic to people and understanding what people need, there is a complete extreme ideology” among Republicans, he said. For Savage-Radich, there have never been clearer choices. “I would never vote for Ramaswamy, I don’t believe anything he says – I don’t believe anything any Republican says right now because every time I fact-check something, they’re lying,” she said. “And now we’re like buddies with China? It’s all crazy. I thought Republicans were the party that was so against China?” She said she doesn’t know a lot about Acton, the Democratic candidate. Republicans have attacked her for enacting Covid-related restrictions during the pandemic, but Savage-Radich noted she was working as the director of the Ohio department of health under a Republican governor. “She didn’t do anything that Mike DeWine didn’t have her do, and that’s a Republican governor,” she said. “To be honest, I think I’m going to vote Democrat all the way down, for everything. Because I want it not to be this way.”

webTitle: Outgoing prison chief in Christa Pike case oversaw five ‘botched’ executions, lawyers say

fields.headline: Outgoing prison chief in Christa Pike case oversaw five ‘botched’ executions, lawyers say
fields.trailText: Frank Strada will leave role next month after uproar over execution attempt, which sent Pike to hospital in critical condition
fields.bodyText: Tennessee’s prison chief is resigning after the failed execution of Christa Pike, which lawyers say was the fifth “botched” execution under his leadership across two states since 2022. Frank Strada, the commissioner of the Tennessee department of correction, has faced mounting questions about the state’s highly secretive death penalty protocols since Wednesday evening when Pike became the first death row prisoner in the US to to be injected with lethal drugs and survive. Witnesses said Pike, 50, was heard choking and struggling an hour after receiving the first injection of pentobarbital, a sedative, and after a second dose failed to kill her she was hospitalized in critical condition. The scrutiny on Strada comes as Pike’s failed execution has sparked international outrage, with lawyers and advocates calling for a national halt on executions in the US. Pike’s lawyers have called the process “cruel and torturous”, and one death penalty expert said it was the worst botched execution in modern history. Bill Lee, Tennessee’s Republican governor, on Saturday announced that Strada would step down from his role this month, the Associated Press reported. Lee also suspended executions in the state until the end of the year and ordered an independent inquiry. Strada said in a statement that stepping aside would “be in the best interests” of the state as the independent review was carried out to determine why Pike’s execution failed on Wednesday. Lee called the case “deeply disturbing”, but when a reporter asked him about Strada’s leadership on Friday, Lee responded: “So far as we know, the department of correction followed exactly the protocol that was outlined.” The journalist was pressing the governor on Strada’s history, which includes another failed execution in May of this year, when Tennessee officials struggled for more than an hour to locate Tony Carruthers’ vein, prompting the procedure to be called off. And when Strada was a deputy prison director in Arizona in 2022, the state carried out three executions that experts and attorneys said were prolonged and “botched”. Death penalty lawyers said there were common threads in the five problematic executions under Strada, including the prisoners’ protracted suffering and questionable injection procedures, and argued that Lee should never have appointed Strada given his Arizona record. Tennessee department of correction spokespeople declined to answer questions about Strada’s record on Friday and said the commissioner was unavailable for an interview. A spokesperson for Lee did not respond to inquiries. ‘Botched’ executions in Arizona After joining Arizona’s corrections department in 2020, Strada oversaw executions, which included forming the teams that carried out the procedures, monitoring the practices and obtaining lethal injection drugs, he said in a deposition. In the May 2022 execution of Clarence Dixon in Arizona, a media witness said the execution team struggled to place IVs to administer the lethal drugs, ultimately requiring them to make an incision by his groin to insert the IV. That process, according to his attorneys, took roughly 40 minutes. In June 2022, a witness said Frank Atwood, a death row prisoner, had to help executioners find a vein after officials repeatedly struggled to kill the 66-year-old, who had a degenerative spinal condition. And in November 2022, Arizona officials struggled to find a vein in Murray Hooper, forcing them to insert a catheter into his groin. The Death Penalty Information Center, a non-profit organization that studies capital punishment, classified all three Arizona executions as “botched”, based on researchers’ analysis. “Botched” is not a legal term, but the group says executions can be botched when there is a breakdown in protocol or unexpected problems or delays that cause needless suffering. Dale Baich, who represented Arizona death row prisoners during Strada’s tenure, said the fact that execution officials’ struggled to find veins suggested they were not qualified: “If your job is to access veins, you should be able to do that ... to me, it indicated the department of corrections did not properly vet those team members.” In a 2023 declaration in a court case, Arizona’s corrections director said his review of execution procedures identified “several critical issues”, including “inadequate knowledge and expertise” of the people involved in executions, concerns about the IV team’s procedures, and concerns about the efficacy of the drugs. Trouble in Tennessee Despite reports of three botched Arizona executions, Lee appointed Strada to head Tennessee’s prisons in early 2023. That appointment came while Tennessee was grappling with its own scandals around lethal injections, with a 2022 state-commissioned independent report finding that Tennessee had failed to follow protocol in several executions, not properly tested drugs and had a “tunnel-vision, result-oriented” approach to executions. Death row attorneys have argued that Strada has failed to address the problems raised in that report. Under Strada, Tennessee removed a key training requirement for people involved in lethal injections, according to Kit Thomas, a death row attorney. Before Strada joined, execution team members were directed to practice catheterization with saline, records show. But training guidelines put in place under Strada eliminated that requirement, saying: “No IV is inserted into the person playing the role of the inmate.” “He reduced the training requirements and we’ve seen disastrous results,” said Thomas. “He oversaw executions in Arizona which involved prolonged, torturous attempts to establish IV lines, and he brought a similar practice here.” After Strada left Arizona, corrections officials made changes to the state’s lethal injection process, including increasing the number of people on the IV team responsible for injections and requiring more rigorous training, records show. But Strada has not overseen similar changes in Tennessee, instead implementing a protocol that mirrored the older Arizona policy of requiring only two people on the IV team that does injections, Thomas noted. Thomas also provided excerpts of a November 2025 deposition where Strada was questioned by death row attorneys. When Strada was asked what he considered to be a successful execution, he responded: “The condemned is put to death.” When a lawyer followed up, asking: “Anything else?”, Strada replied: “No.” Thomas said Strada’s response suggested he had “no regard for the experience of the individual being executed other than that they end up dead”. The response, she added, echoed the same “tunnel-vision” approach to executions that investigators had called out in the Tennessee-commissioned report in 2022. In the 2025 deposition, Strada further acknowledged he had not followed some of the recommendations of the 2022 report, including failing to hire a full-time employee or consultant with a pharmaceutical background to provide guidance on the lethal injection process and failing to hire a full-time employee or consultant to assist with locating lethal injection sources. “What good is an independent investigation if those investigators provide recommendations that are ignored?” said Thomas. Questions mount over lethal drugs Questions about how the state acquires, maintains and administers lethal injection drugs are critical following the botched killing of Pike, who was sentenced to death in 1996 at age 20 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Pike’s lawyers said Friday that she remained unconscious and on a ventilator. Prison officials have not addressed questions of what might have gone wrong, but some outside experts have questioned whether the pentobarbital could have been degraded or may have failed to properly enter her bloodstream and instead seeped into surrounding tissue. Tennessee keeps secret the identities of people involved in executions and basic facts about the drugs it uses in executions. Thomas pointed to a number of questions that Strada previously declined to answer, including whether he was using the same drug supplier he used in Arizona, whether Tennessee’s supplier had complied with Food and Drug Administration rules and regulations, and whether he had any procedures or checklists to ensure the lethal injection chemicals had not been adulterated. Stephen Ferrell, federal defender and one of Pike’s attorneys, expressed skepticism about the governor’s call for another independent inquiry, noting the last independent investigation on the state’s death penalty system resulted in continued secrecy. “We are kept in the dark,” he said in a press conference Thursday, noting that reporters who served as witnesses to Pike’s botched killing also raised concerns about the secrecy surrounding the execution procedure: “Our predictions are downplayed, and yet they continue to come true. Tennessee should not be torturing its citizens in the name of justice.” As the governor sidestepped questions about Strada, candidates running to replace Lee said they would not keep Strada in the job if they were elected in the November midterms. Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said Tennessee officials should answer questions about Strada’s involvement in multiple botched executions. She also raised concerns about the lack of transparency or accountability after Carruthers’ botched execution in May: “We saw no information about why this had gone wrong and no explanation or corrective action to ensure that wouldn’t happen another time.” “Governor Lee should urge his officials to be forthcoming about all the mistakes that may have been made and to accept responsibility for whatever went wrong with these executions,” she continued. Ed Pilkington contributed reporting

webTitle: A billionaire is one of Trump’s loudest critics. Will Democrats send him to the White House?

fields.headline: A billionaire is one of Trump’s loudest critics. Will Democrats send him to the White House?
fields.trailText: As the Illinois governor seeks a third term, his growing national profile has fueled speculation about a possible White House bid
fields.bodyText: When Donald Trump returned to power, 20 long months ago, some state leaders wrung their hands, worrying what explicit resistance might cost their citizens – and their careers – during the second term of a vengeful president. JB Pritzker was not among them. Two days after Trump’s re-election, the Democratic governor of Illinois warned the president would need to “come through me” to reach the people of his state. He waited all of 30 days after the inauguration before drawing a comparison with Nazi Germany. “All I’m saying”, Pritzker declared during his State of the State address in February 2025, “is when the five-alarm fire starts to burn, every good person better be ready to man a post with a bucket of water if you want to stop it from raging out of control”. Not everyone grabbed a bucket. While Pritzker is willing to cede that he was not entirely alone in standing up to Trump in those early months, prominent figures alongside him could be counted “on each of your digits”, he suggests in an interview at his campaign headquarters in Chicago. Several of his counterparts – from Gavin Newsom, who launched a legislative blitz to curb immigration enforcement in California, to Janet Mills of Maine, who told Trump she would see him in court over his bid to deny state funding over transgender athletes – could legitimately claim a digit. Others have taken an altogether different tack. New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani is among those who have sought to strike a productive working relationship with the president. And in Washington, Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer faced fierce criticism after some Democratic senators reached a bipartisan deal to end the longest-ever US government shutdown. Now, Pritzker suggests, the number of elected leaders willing to speak out aggressively against the administration is “finally” growing. “For one reason or another, people have chosen to come on board with Team Fight, and get off of Team Cave.” Trump and Pritzker have a few things in common. Both are billionaires who inherited enormous wealth from their families. Both worked in business before entering politics. Both – no, the comparison pretty much ends there, says Pritzker, who, according to the governor’s campaign, has not spoken to Trump since the Covid pandemic. “He’s a wannabe authoritarian, and I don’t say that rhetorically,” argues Pritzker, a philanthropist who helped build his state’s Holocaust Museum before entering office and spent time with survivors. “One thing that they would tell you is that you cannot give an authoritarian an inch.” The governor is regularly cited as a potential contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nominee – encouraged, however implicitly, by his self-appointment as captain of Team Fight in Illinois. Amid visceral anger among voters over the political status quo – not just at one party, or one president, but the sustained failure to fix big problems and improve their lives – could he do this job nationwide? He has another election to win first. Illinois is one of 36 states with gubernatorial elections coming in November. Pritzker is widely expected to become the state’s first three-term governor in more than three decades. (His Republican opponent, state senator Darren Bailey, finished 12 points behind last time around.) Pritzker, first elected during Trump’s first term, says his tenure has been dominated by four crises: a fiscal quagmire inherited from his Republican predecessor; the Covid-19 pandemic; Texas governor Greg Abbott’s move to send tens of thousands of migrants to Chicago; and Trump’s return. All the while, he says, he has focused on affordability and the rights of Illinoisans, from raising the state minimum wage to codifying reproductive rights. After a string of credit rating upgrades, Pritzker likens alleviating the state’s financial woes process to reorienting an aircraft carrier 180 degrees – something he claims to have done, although critics note Illinois retains one of the lowest ratings in the country. With Democrats hoping to use November’s midterm elections to mount a significant fightback against Trump, Pritzker launched a $20m political action committee to support party campaigns nationwide, recently flew to Texas to help counter-program the Republican convention, and will soon head to South Carolina, the first state in Democrats’ next presidential nominating process, to address the NAACP state conference. His job might be in the state of Illinois, but his career aspirations sure look national. *** Time is slowly but surely ticking on the Trump era. With the president barred by the US constitution from running for a third term, the searing political spotlight will soon shift, whether he likes it or not, on to those vying to succeed him. As Democrats search for a candidate who could win back the White House and confine this chapter to the history books, speculation around Pritzker’s aspirations stepped up a level last week when he disclosed he has been using a GLP-1 medication to lose weight over the past two years. Pritzker “knows what a lot of people may be thinking”, reported CBS News, which broke the news. “Eyeing a 2028 Bid, He Used a Weight-Loss Drug to Drop 80 Pounds,” ran the New York Times headline. “Ahead of Possible Presidential Bid, JB Pritzker Says He Is Taking Weight-Loss Drugs,” offered the Wall Street Journal. Just how many times has he been asked if he’s running for president? For the first time in our hour together, Pritzker hesitates. “I’m not sure the connection,” he replies. “National political reporters can’t help yourselves,” he adds, referring to the way the announcement about his health was covered. “I’m not sure the question. You’re asking … what are you asking me?” How many times has Pritzker – a politician who argues Democrats should campaign nationally on issues he so happens to have championed in his state – been asked if he’s running for president? “Reporters that don’t know me” continue to ask “very often”, he concedes. “I understand why people ask the question,” he continues, pointing to his record in Illinois. The conspicuous lack of a firm answer might also have something to do with it. He is more open to discussing what exactly went wrong at the last election, and the factors behind the crushing defeat suffered by Kamala Harris in 2024. Beyond the “entire setup” of Joe Biden’s withdrawal 15 weeks before polling day, Pritzker wishes the campaign had focused more on “putting money in people’s pockets”, citing an increase in the national minimum wage, which has stood at $7.25 per hour since 2009. “People need to hear that you’re going to do something tangible for them today, immediately. “I think the campaign should have entirely been about working families, the middle class, people striving to get there, and the most vulnerable,” says Pritzker. “And I often say those things – I mean, I talk about those people – because that’s why I’m a Democrat. And it’s why, I think, most people are Democrats, or would vote for a Democrat.” It is also, perhaps coincidentally, one of the key areas where Pritzker says he has delivered in Illinois. From the outset as governor, he took the view that he should be “fighting for the things that in your everyday life are challenging, fighting to overcome those challenges, and fighting for things that make it a little easier”, he says. Even in campaign mode, he acknowledges one failure: his signature plan to overhaul the state’s tax system from a flat rate to a graduated levy, which was rejected by voters in 2020. While Pritzker has endured his fair share of attacks and potshots as governor, not least from Trump, a presidential run would bring a whole new layer of scrutiny – of his record, his background, and his wealth. An heir to the Hyatt hotel chain who ran an investment firm with his brother before running for governor, Pritzker’s personal fortune currently stands at about $4.2bn, according to Forbes: significantly more than Trump’s fortune before his return to office, albeit significantly less than Trump’s fortune today. In 2024, Pritzker made more than $1.4m while playing blackjack on vacation. “I was incredibly lucky,” he said at a press conference at the time. “It was in Las Vegas, and I like to play cards,” he added as an explanation. We’ve all been there. (The governor’s campaign said he donated the winnings to charity.) This year’s Democratic primaries have been dominated by headlines about anti-establishment, anti-elite candidates – including some members of the Democratic Socialists of America, or DSA – clinching the party’s nominations, from Michigan and Pennsylvania to New York and Florida. Pritzker has been watching closely. “I think there is a desperate need for elected officials to address affordability,” he says. “And the candidates that are winning are the ones who are communicating their passion for the issue, and their articulation of the policies that will bring that. I think if you’re not showing up with that, then you’re missing the point.” Sure, Pritzker cedes across the boardroom table; “some national reporters” have “focused” on DSA victories. “But I will just point out to you that that’s a very, relatively small percentage of the results in primaries,” he suggests. “Although they’re notable.” “The more outspoken people, even if they weren’t DSA members, I think won,” he adds. “And they won because that is what people are feeling. People are hurting, genuinely pained, right now.” A notable number of Democratic candidates won the party’s nomination by speaking out not only for those struggling to make ends meet – but also against those at the other end of the spectrum, with extreme wealth. Is today’s Democratic party really prepared to send a billionaire to the White House? Pritzker allows a brief chuckle. “Could we rephrase that question? Because you’re trying to single me out, I think,” he says. “How about if we say it a little – I’ll just answer it the way I want to.” “When I ran in [the Illinois gubernatorial] Democratic primary in 2018, people asked the question, do we really want a businessman billionaire to be our Democratic candidate for governor? I think a legitimate question, given … what people were seeing,” he says, pointing again to Trump, but also Bruce Rauner, the former Republican Illinois governor – a mere multimillionaire at the time – whom he went on to defeat. “Legitimate question today,” acknowledges Pritzker. “Look at Elon Musk. Look at Sam Altman. Look at – we could make a list, whoever you want to fit in what sometimes people refer to as ‘the oligarchs’ in that group. I understand the skepticism that people have about wealthy people. “But what I can tell you is that, over the course of the last eight years – and I think over the course of my life, really, but certainly as people have paid more attention over the last eight years – I’ve proven that I have, in fact, done more for working people in this state than maybe any governor in the country, and … restored services for the most vulnerable people in our state. “And so the real question is, what are your values? Not how much money do you have, but what do you believe?”

webTitle: Trump threatens to double tariffs on South Korea if they do not pay for Alaska natural gas pipeline – as it happened

fields.headline: Trump threatens to double tariffs on South Korea if they do not pay for Alaska natural gas pipeline – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: This concludes our live coverage of the second Trump administration for the day. Here are the latest developments: Confronted with the fact that South Korean officials say they did not agree to invest $54bn to build a natural gas pipeline in Alaska, as Donald Trump announced they had on Wednesday, the president threatened to double tariffs on South Korean goods imported to the US unless they agree to make the investment. Ignoring public sentiment, that his war with Iran and failure to tackle inflation has hurt the country, Trump told supporters in Alabama that his second term is “the most successful presidency in history.” Trump regaled supporters in Alabama with a version of his rally speech that included many of his familiar boasts and grievances, a number of which were based on entirely imaginary claims previously debunked by the Guardian. A federal judge blocked the Trump administration from constructing a border wall at Big Bend national park in Texas until a lawsuit opposing it is resolved. Ignoring the economic anxiety of the public, Trump boasted to reporters at the White House that his new helipad is “getting all sorts of awards” and described a massive crane towering over the ballroom he is constructing as “pretty cool”. Senator Adam Schiff reaffirmed his support on Friday for legislation introduced this week by Democrats that would stop the Trump administration from closing archives of government records in California and Illinois. “The administration is threatening access to historical and irreplaceable records, including closing down one facility in California that is home to countless photos and family heirlooms,” Schiff said in a statement. “Congress must exercise its oversight power to save decades of regional and national history.” Schiff and his California colleague Alex Padilla joined two Illinois Democrats, Tammy Duckworth and Dick Durbin, to introduce the National Archives Protection Act, which would ensure archival records remain accessible to the public. One of the facilities the administration reportedly plans to close, in the San Francisco Bay area, hosts original records from the US supreme court case United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which affirmed that the constitution grants birthright citizenship to anyone born in the US. The blessed sound of YMCA has just been heard in Mobile, Alabama, signaling that Donald Trump’s rally speech is over. In his remarks, which included a plea to supporters to “just close your eyes and pretend I’m on the ballot,” Trump mentioned various Republican candidates in passing, but mainly made the case for himself, casting his second term in office as an unalloyed triumph, marred only by “bad press”. “If you want to keep America the strongest, most successful nation the world has ever seen – we are right now more respected than at any time in the history of our country, and that’s where the bad press,” Trump said, “you have to vote Republican.” “Just think of what the Trump administration and our Republican majorities have accomplished in less than two years’ time,” he went on. “Nobody’s ever seen this before. Nobody’s ever done it. We have the most successful- it’s not two years; it’s substantially less - the most successful presidency in history.” Late in the speech, Trump named Republican candidates and elected officials who were on hand, including senator Katie Britt, who achieved viral fame this week for the look of horror on her face as her colleague Eric Schmitt badly botched an attempt to make former special counsel Jack Smith look bad. Trump then singled out the far-right, anti-Muslim influencer Laura Loomer for praise. “A great Republican strategist, a great person, a killer,” Trump said. “When she’s angry at you, it’s a very terrible situation. Laura Loomer. Thank you. Laura. She’s great.” Loomer, an influential outside Trump adviser whose extreme views and statements led to criticism of Trump during the 2024 campaign, when she traveled with him to events, posted a photograph of herself with Trump on Air Force One earlier in the day. Donald Trump is regaling supporters in Alabama with a version of his rally speech that includes many of his familiar boasts and grievances, a number of which are based on entirely imaginary claims. To take one example, Trump once again claimed that he was instantly blamed for high prices by the media after just one day in office. “I took over and in my first news conference on January 21st … a day after that beautiful day we had in quite cold weather, the inauguration. A day later, I had a news conference and they said, ‘affordability’. I said, ‘I just got here. What do they mean?’” Trump insisted, despite the fact that he was, in fact, asked no questions about affordability at all during that news conference. In the first weeks of his administration, Trump repeatedly claimed that prices were dropping and then, at a cabinet meeting two months into his second term, claimed for the first time that he had been unfairly blamed for high egg prices. “When I came in, after one week, they were screaming at me about eggs. Eggs had nothing to do with me,” the president said on 24 March 2025. He has repeated the false claim that reporters blamed him for high food prices dozens of times since. Later in the address, Trump said, as he has dozens of times since he visited Saudi Arabia in May 2025, that the Saudi king had praised him for almost instantly turning around the US economy. “Less than two years ago, our country was dead,” Trump told supporters in Alabama on Friday night. “Remember that? I told you, the king of Saudi Arabia was talking to me. He said, you know, ‘Sir, just a short time ago, your country was dead. The whole Middle East, the whole world was laughing at you. And now you have the hottest country anywhere in the world.’” As the Guardian has reported previously, Trump did not meet the Saudi king, who is elderly and not often seen in public, during his visit last year. Instead, he was hosted by the Saudi crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman. There is also no evidence that the Saudi prince made this statement to Trump, but there is video of Trump making a version of that claim to bin Salman during an address to a US-Saudi investment event in Riyadh on 13 May 2025. “The days of economic misery under the last administration are rapidly giving way to the greatest economy in the history of the world,” Trump said before directly addressing the crown prince in the audience. “We are rocking. The United States is the hottest country, with the exception of your country, I have to say, right? … No Mohammed… You’re hotter. At least as long as I’m up here, you’re hotter. But groceries, gasoline, energy and all other prices are down with no inflation. We have no inflation.” Two weeks after his return to the US, Trump began saying that this observation had been made not by him, but to him. “I went to Saudi Arabia,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on 28 May 2025. “The king told me, he said, ‘you got the hottest com-’ we have the hottest country in the world right now.,” Trump said. “Six months ago this country was stone cold dead. We had a dead country.” As he repeated the story, again and again, Trump began to also attribute his own claim, that the US was “dead” under Joe Biden, to the Saudi king as well. In remarks at the Nato summit in the Hague in June 2025, Trump insisted that the Saudi king had told him: “A year ago, your country was dead. You had a deadhead running it. You had a country that was dead”. Since then, Trump has repeated the tale dozens of times.
